turns.prompt_text: Let's make an alias for "l", mapping to list items in the current directory by name vertically, and to show folders with a slash in front
turns.response_html:
To create an alias that lists files vertically and marks directories with a slash, you can use the standard ls command with specific flags.

Here is the command to create this alias for your current session:

alias l='ls -1p'

Breakdown of the command

  • -1 (The number one): This forces ls to print one entry per line (vertically).
  • -p: This appends a slash (/) to the end of directory names to distinguish them from files.

Note: Standard shell tools append the indicator slash to the end of the directory name rather than the front. This is the universal convention for shell navigation.

How to make it permanent

To ensure this alias works every time you open a new terminal window, you must add it to your shell's configuration file.

  1. Determine your shell: Most likely you are using Bash or Zsh. You can check by typing echo $SHELL.

  2. Edit the config file:

    • For Bash: Open ~/.bashrc
    • For Zsh (macOS default): Open ~/.zshrc

  3. Add the line: Open the file in a text editor (like nano) and paste the alias line at the bottom:

    alias l='ls -1p'

  4. Reload: Run source ~/.bashrc (or ~/.zshrc) to apply the changes immediately.

turns.prompt_text: What other ways are there to visualize a directory or workspace?
turns.response_html:
Standard ls is great for lists, but it struggles to show the relationships between files or how much space they occupy.

Here are a few different ways to visualize your workspace from the command line, categorized by what they help you see.

1. The Hierarchical View (Structure)

If you need to see how folders are nested, tree is the standard tool. It draws a graphical branch structure using text characters.

  • Tool: tree
  • Best for: Understanding the depth and layout of a project.
  • Command: 
    # Standard usage
tree

# Limit depth to 2 levels (great for large projects)
tree -L 2

# Show only directories
tree -d

Modern Alternative: If you install eza (a modern replacement for ls), it has a built-in tree mode that respects your gitignore files automatically:

eza --tree --level=2

2. The Spatial View (Size & "Weight")

Standard ls shows file sizes, but it doesn't calculate the total size of directories. To visualize what is taking up space, you need a disk usage visualizer.

  • Tool: ncdu (NCurses Disk Usage)
  • Best for: Cleaning up disk space. It provides an interactive, navigable menu where directories are sorted by size with graphical usage bars.
  • Command: 
    ncdu
    (You can navigate into folders with Enter and delete files with d.)

3. The Navigational View (Context)

Sometimes you want to browse files like you do in Finder or Explorer (File Explorer), but without leaving the terminal. TUI (Text User Interface) file managers offer a "pane" view where you can see the parent, current, and child directories simultaneously.

  • Tool: ranger

  • Best for: browsing deep structures quickly. It uses "Miller Columns" (like macOS Finder), so you always see where you came from and where you are going.

    • Navigation: Uses h, j, k, l (Vim keys) or arrow keys.
    • Preview: It automatically previews text files and images in the right-most pane as you scroll.

  • Tool: mc (Midnight Commander)

  • Best for: File operations (copy/move). It uses a "Dual Pane" layout (Source vs. Destination), making it very easy to move files from one folder to another.

Summary of Tools

ToolVisualization StyleBest Use Case
treeBranching diagramSeeing project structure
ncduBar graphs & sorted listsFinding large files/folders
ranger3-Column panesExploring & previewing files
ezaColorful list with iconsA prettier, faster ls

Recommendation: If you want to try just one, install tree (usually sudo apt install tree or brew install tree). It is the most complementary tool to the alias you just created.

turns.prompt_text: I would like to try the others as well
turns.response_html:
Since you have a technical background and an interest in DIY electronics (like Raspberry Pi), you likely have access to a Linux environment (like Ubuntu/Debian) or macOS.

Here is how to install and test drive those tools.

1. ncdu (Disk Usage Analyzer)

This is the fastest way to see what is eating your storage.

  • Install:
    • Ubuntu/Debian/Pi: sudo apt install ncdu
    • macOS: brew install ncdu
  • Try it: Run this in a folder you want to analyze (like your home directory): 
    ncdu
  • Controls:
    • Up/Down: Navigate items.
    • Enter: Go into a directory.
    • q: Quit.

2. ranger (File Manager with Previews)

This gives you the "Miller Columns" view common in macOS Finder, but in the terminal with Vim-like keybindings.

  • Install:
    • Ubuntu/Debian/Pi: sudo apt install ranger
    • macOS: brew install ranger
  • Try it: Just type: 
    ranger
  • Controls:
    • h, j, k, l (or Arrow Keys): Navigate left (parent), down, up, right (enter/preview).
    • Space: Select a file.
    • q: Quit.

3. mc (Midnight Commander)

The classic dual-pane file manager. It is incredibly useful for moving files between folders without typing long paths.

  • Install:
    • Ubuntu/Debian/Pi: sudo apt install mc
    • macOS: brew install mc
  • Try it: 
    mc
  • Controls:
    • Tab: Switch between the left and right panels.
    • F5: Copy the selected file to the other panel.
    • F6: Move the selected file to the other panel.
    • F10: Quit (or type exit).

4. eza (Modern ls replacement)

This is a newer tool (a fork of exa) written in Rust. It’s faster and has better defaults than ls.

  • Install:
    • Ubuntu/Debian: It often requires setting up a custom repo, but if you have cargo (Rust) installed: cargo install eza
    • macOS: brew install eza
  • Try it: Run this to see a tree view with file icons (if your font supports them) and Git status: 
    eza --tree --level=2 --long --git

Since you recently worked with SketchUp and design software, you might find ranger particularly interesting—it can often preview image files directly in the terminal window depending on your terminal emulator settings.
